mcqs.question: What's the core structural difference between how CommonJS's `require` and ES Modules' `import` resolve, independent of syntax?
options: `require` can only load JSON files, while `import` can load any file type
`import` is always faster at runtime because it uses a binary format internally
There is no real structural difference — they're just two spellings of the same mechanism
`require` runs as a synchronous function call at the point it appears; `import`/`export` are static declarations resolved before any module code executes
mcqs.explanation: CommonJS treats `require` as an ordinary function call executed wherever it appears in the code, while ESM's `import`/`export` are hoisted, statically-analyzable declarations resolved ahead of execution. That structural difference — not file-type support or raw speed — is what the rest of the topic (tree-shaking, circular imports) builds on.

mcqs.question: Why can't a bundler reliably tree-shake a CommonJS module the way it can an ES Module?
options: `require(someVariable)` can determine what to load only at runtime, so a bundler can't always know which exports are used without actually executing the program
CommonJS modules are always larger in file size than ES Modules
Tree-shaking is a feature bundlers deliberately disable for CommonJS for licensing reasons
CommonJS doesn't support the `export` keyword at all, making analysis impossible
mcqs.explanation: Tree-shaking requires proving statically, without running the program, which exports are actually used. CommonJS's dynamic `require` calls can depend on runtime values, so that proof generally isn't possible — the bundler has to conservatively assume more of the module might be needed. This is a structural limitation, not a licensing choice or a keyword-support gap.

mcqs.question: Module A and Module B `require` each other (a circular dependency) in CommonJS. If B is loaded partway through A's initial execution, what does B receive when it requires A?
options: A fully-populated `module.exports` for A, since Node resolves circular dependencies before running any module code
Whatever `module.exports` looks like at that exact moment — potentially incomplete, since A hasn't finished running yet
A runtime error, since CommonJS forbids circular requires entirely
An empty object, since circular requires always reset exports to their initial state
mcqs.explanation: CommonJS resolves eagerly and synchronously, so a circular `require` returns a snapshot of `module.exports` exactly as it stood at that moment — which can be missing properties A hasn't assigned yet. Node doesn't forbid circular requires or reset exports; it returns the partial object as-is, which is the actual hazard to watch for.

mcqs.question: Why do some style guides prefer named exports over default exports, even for files that export just one thing?
options: Default exports are deprecated in the ECMAScript standard

Named exports enforce a fixed, consistent name at every import site and support more precise tree-shaking; a default export's importer can rename it freely, letting the same thing get called different names across a codebase
Named exports run faster at import time than default exports
Default exports cannot be used with `import()` dynamic imports
mcqs.explanation: Because a default export carries no fixed name, every import site can choose its own local name for it, which drifts inconsistently across a large codebase, and tooling-assisted renames are less reliable. Neither export style is deprecated, faster, or restricted from dynamic import — the trade-off is about naming consistency and refactor tooling, not runtime behavior.

mcqs.question: An app imports only `Button` from a barrel file (`index.js` re-exporting an entire components directory), but the final bundle still includes an unrelated, huge charting library also re-exported from that same barrel. What's the most likely cause?
options: The bundler is broken and needs to be reconfigured from scratch
Barrel files always disable minification for the whole app
Named imports from barrel files are silently converted into default imports, pulling in everything

The bundler couldn't prove the other re-exported modules have no side effects, so it conservatively included the barrel's full transitive dependency tree rather than risk dropping something with a side effect
mcqs.explanation: Barrel files can defeat tree-shaking because proving a re-exported module has no side effects requires more static analysis than a direct named import — many bundlers fall back to including everything the barrel touches rather than risk incorrectly eliminating a module with side effects. This has nothing to do with minification being disabled or named imports being converted to default imports.

mcqs.question: Tree-shaking is best described as which combination of steps?
options: Minifying variable names, followed by gzip compression

Statically building the module graph to know exactly which exports are used, then removing anything never imported by anything reachable from the entry point — the same idea as removing an unreachable `if (false)` branch
Randomly sampling which exports are used at runtime and removing the rest based on frequency
Splitting every file into its own separate network request regardless of usage
mcqs.explanation: Tree-shaking is dead-code elimination applied to the module graph: build a precise picture of what's actually imported (possible because ESM is statically analyzable), then strip anything provably unreachable from the entry point. It has nothing to do with minification, gzip, runtime sampling, or splitting every file into separate requests — that's code-splitting, a related but distinct concern.
